format: General Training: TRUE/FALSE/NOT GIVEN
passage:
Citizen Science: When Everyone Can Be a Researcher

A  Scientific research is often imagined as the work of professionals in laboratories, but some of the largest data sets in modern science have been collected by people with no formal training at all. Known as citizen science, this approach invites members of the public to take part in research by counting birds, classifying images, recording the weather or even playing computer games. Thanks to the internet and smartphones, the number of such projects has grown enormously in recent decades, and millions of people around the world now contribute to them.

B  The idea is not new. One of the longest-running examples, the Christmas Bird Count, began in North America in 1900. At the time, it was a popular holiday tradition for hunters to compete to see who could shoot the most birds in a day. An ornithologist named Frank Chapman suggested that people should count birds instead of killing them, and on the first count, a few dozen volunteers took part. Today, tens of thousands of people take part each year, and the records they have accumulated over more than a century have helped scientists to track how bird populations and ranges have changed.

C  The internet transformed what citizen scientists could do. In 2007, astronomers launched a website called Galaxy Zoo, which asked members of the public to classify images of galaxies according to their shape. The researchers had expected the task to take years; instead, volunteers made millions of classifications within the first year, and in several cases their careful observations led to genuine discoveries. Most famously, a Dutch schoolteacher noticed an unusual green cloud of gas near a galaxy, an object that had never been described before and that now bears her name.

D  Some projects take the form of games. In one online puzzle game, players fold virtual models of proteins, competing to find the most stable shapes. In 2011, players produced a model of an enzyme from a monkey virus similar to HIV, a problem that had puzzled scientists for many years, within a matter of weeks. The success demonstrated that human intuition and spatial reasoning can sometimes outperform computer programs, particularly when large numbers of people work on a problem together.

E  Professional scientists sometimes worry about the reliability of data collected by amateurs. Volunteers may misidentify species, record observations inconsistently or concentrate on easily accessible locations. Well-designed projects address these concerns in several ways: they provide clear instructions and training, ask several volunteers to classify the same item, and use experts or computer checks to flag unusual records. Studies comparing volunteer and professional data have found that, with such safeguards, the quality is often comparable.

F  For participants, the rewards are varied. Many enjoy learning about a subject they find fascinating, and some report that regular observation of nature improves their well-being. Others value the sense of contributing to something larger than themselves. Researchers increasingly recognise that citizen science can also strengthen public understanding of how science works and build trust between scientists and the communities they study. As one project leader has put it, the aim is not simply to obtain free labour, but to make science something that people do rather than something that is done to them.

format: General Training: TRUE/FALSE/NOT GIVEN
passage:
Ashford Volunteer Centre: Current Opportunities

A  Hospital Welcome Desk. Greet patients and visitors at the main entrance of Ashford General Hospital and help them find their way. Shifts last three hours, on weekday mornings. Volunteers must be over 18 and will need a background check, which we will arrange.

B  Riverside Clean-Up. Join our monthly Saturday morning litter-pick along the River Ash. Gloves, litter pickers and refreshments are provided. No experience is needed, and under-16s are welcome if accompanied by an adult.

C  Reading Buddies. Spend one hour a week listening to children read at a local primary school. Training is given before you start. A minimum commitment of one school year is requested.

D  Charity Shop Assistant. Help sort donations, price items and serve customers in our town-centre shop. Flexible hours; ideal for anyone wanting retail experience for their CV.

E  Befriending Service. Make a weekly phone call or home visit to an older person who lives alone. Volunteers are matched with someone who shares their interests. Travel expenses are reimbursed.

explanation: A「will need a background check, which we will arrange」。センターが 手配するので FALSE。

Halden Consulting: Claiming Business Expenses

A  What you can claim. You may claim reasonable costs incurred while travelling on company business, including public transport fares, mileage for using your own car, accommodation and meals. Travel between your home and your usual place of work cannot be claimed.

B  Mileage. If you use your own car, you can claim 45p per mile for the first 10,000 business miles in a tax year. You must keep a record of the date, purpose and distance of each journey.

C  Meals. When you are away from your usual workplace for more than five hours, you may claim up to £10 for a meal. If you are away overnight, the limit is £30 for an evening meal. Alcoholic drinks cannot be claimed.

D  Receipts. Original receipts must be attached to every claim, except for car mileage. Photographs of receipts are acceptable if they are clear and complete.

E  Deadlines. Claims must be submitted through the finance system within 60 days of the expense. Late claims will only be accepted in exceptional circumstances, with the approval of a director.

format: General Training: TRUE/FALSE/NOT GIVEN
passage:
The Return of the Night Train

A  Not long ago, the overnight passenger train seemed to be heading for extinction in Europe. As low-cost airlines expanded and high-speed rail lines shortened daytime journeys, demand for sleeper services fell, and operators cut routes that had run for decades. In 2016, Germany's national railway company withdrew from operating night trains altogether, arguing that they had become unprofitable. Few observers at the time would have predicted that, within a few years, night trains would be enjoying a revival.

B  Much of the credit belongs to Austria's national railway, which took over several of the routes abandoned in Germany and relaunched them under a new brand. It invested in modernising its carriages and marketed the service as a comfortable and environmentally friendly alternative to flying. At the same time, public attitudes were changing. Concern about the climate impact of air travel grew rapidly in the late 2010s, and in Sweden a new word was coined to describe the guilt some people felt about flying. Rail operators found a growing market of travellers willing to spend a night on a train to avoid a short-haul flight.

C  Since then, new routes have connected cities such as Vienna, Paris, Brussels, Berlin and Amsterdam, and several new companies have entered the market. For passengers, the appeal is easy to understand. A traveller can board in one city in the evening, sleep, and arrive in another city centre in the morning, without the need to travel to an airport, pass through security or pay for a hotel. Many also simply enjoy the experience, which some compare to the romance of rail travel in earlier eras.

D  Running night trains, however, is far from easy. Sleeping cars carry far fewer passengers than ordinary carriages, so revenue per train is relatively low, while costs are high: trains need staff throughout the night, and operators must pay charges to use the tracks in every country they pass through. Rules, signalling systems and even electricity supplies differ between national rail networks, so locomotives or crews sometimes need to be changed at borders. New carriages are expensive and can take years to build, and delays in delivering them have forced some services to run with older equipment.

E  Passengers, too, have complaints. Tickets for private compartments can cost more than a flight, and on some routes late running and last-minute cancellations have damaged the reputation of the service. Supporters argue that governments should do more to help, for example by reducing track charges for night trains or by taxing aviation fuel, which in many cases is exempt from the taxes paid on other fuels.

F  Whether the revival will last remains uncertain. Night trains are unlikely ever to replace air travel over very long distances, and their success depends on a delicate balance of public support, reliable operation and affordable fares. Yet for journeys of between roughly 600 and 1,500 kilometres, they offer a genuine alternative, and many travellers appear ready to give them a chance.
